blocks.title: Our goal
blocks.say: Today we’re adding fractions with different bottom numbers, like 2/3 + 1/4. The bottom number is called the denominator. It tells you how many equal pieces the whole is cut into.

blocks.title: A tempting shortcut
blocks.say: It’s tempting to add the tops and add the bottoms: 2/3 + 1/4 = 3/7. But look at the bars. 3/7 is shorter than 2/3 on its own, and adding something can’t make an amount smaller. So that shortcut can’t be right.

blocks.title: Same-size pieces
blocks.say: Thirds and quarters are different sizes of piece, so 2 thirds + 1 quarter isn’t “3 of anything”. To add fractions, we first have to cut both into pieces of the same size.

blocks.title: Cut both into twelfths
blocks.say: Press the button to cut both bars into 12 equal pieces. 12 works because both 3 and 4 go into it. Now 2/3 is 8 pieces and 1/4 is 3 pieces, and the pieces are the same size.

blocks.title: Now we can add
blocks.say: Both are counted in twelfths, so we can add them: 8 twelfths + 3 twelfths = 11 twelfths. So 2/3 + 1/4 = 11/12.

blocks.title: The method
blocks.say: That’s the whole method, in four moves. Next you’ll watch it done once, then try one yourself.
list: Find a common denominator: a number that both bottoms go into.
Convert: rewrite each fraction with that bottom. Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number.
Add the tops. The bottom stays the same.

lines.say: Let’s add 1/6 + 1/3. The bottoms are different, 6 and 3, so we can’t add yet. I’ll go through the four moves, one line at a time.
Move 1: find a common denominator. 3 goes into 6, and 6 goes into itself, so 6 works for both. That means we can keep 1/6 as it is and only change the other fraction.
Move 2: convert. To get 6 on the bottom of 1/3, we multiply the bottom by 2. So we multiply the top by 2 as well: 1 × 2 = 2. The bars show that 1/3 and 2/6 are the same amount.
Move 3: add the tops. Both are sixths now, so 1 + 2 = 3. The bottom stays 6, because we’re still counting sixths.
Move 4: simplify. 3 and 6 both divide by 3, so divide the top and the bottom by 3: 3 ÷ 3 = 1 and 6 ÷ 3 = 2. That gives 1/2.
So 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/2. Four moves: common denominator, convert, add the tops, simplify. Now it’s your turn.

parts.title: Try one together
parts.intro: Your turn, and I’ll check every line. We’re adding 1/4 + 1/6 with the same four moves.
parts.finish: Well done. 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12. You found a common denominator, converted both fractions, added the tops and checked whether it simplifies. One more, this time on your own.

steps.say: Move 1: find a common denominator, a number that both 4 and 6 go into. Type the smallest one you can find.
steps.multipleNote: {n} works too, because both 4 and 6 go into it. The smallest one keeps the numbers small, so we’ll use 12.

mistakes.say: 6 is in the 6 times table, but 4 doesn’t go into 6 evenly. Keep counting up in sixes.
4 is in the 4 times table, but 6 doesn’t go into 4. You need a bigger number.
Neither 4 nor 6 goes into 10 evenly. Try counting up in sixes and test each number with 4.

hints: Count up in sixes: 6, 12, 18, 24. Which of those does 4 go into?
steps.wrong: Not quite. The number has to be in both the 4 times table and the 6 times table.
steps.why: 12 is in the 4 times table (4 × 3) and in the 6 times table (6 × 2).

steps.say: Move 2: convert. Rewrite 1/4 with 12 on the bottom. What did we multiply 4 by to get 12? Do the same to the top.

mistakes.say: 1 is the old top. The bottom was multiplied, so the top has to be multiplied by the same number, or the fraction would change size.

hints: 4 × 3 = 12, so we multiply by 3. Now do the same to the top: 1 × 3.
steps.wrong: Not quite. Multiply the top by the same number you multiplied the bottom by.
steps.why: We multiplied the bottom by 3 (4 × 3 = 12), so the top is multiplied by 3 too: 1 × 3 = 3. That makes 1/4 = 3/12.

steps.say: Same again for 1/6. What do we multiply 6 by to get 12?

mistakes.say: 1 is the old top. The bottom was multiplied, so the top has to be multiplied by the same number.

steps.wrong: Not quite. Multiply the top by the same number you multiplied the bottom by.
steps.why: 6 × 2 = 12, so the top is 1 × 2 = 2. That makes 1/6 = 2/12.

steps.say: Move 3: both are twelfths now, so we can add. Add the tops. What’s the new top?
hints: The pieces are the same size now, so just count them: 3 pieces plus 2 pieces.
steps.wrong: Not quite. Count the pieces: 3 twelfths plus 2 twelfths.
steps.why: 3 + 2 = 5, so we have 5 twelfths. The bottom stays 12, because we’re still counting twelfths.

steps.say: Move 4: simplify. Is there a number that goes into both 5 and 12? If there isn’t, type the fraction exactly as it is.
steps.ifEquivalent: That’s a bigger fraction with the same value, but simplifying should make the numbers smaller. 5/12 is already as simple as it gets.
hints: Try 2, 3, 4 and 5. Does any of them go into both 5 and 12?
5 is only in the 5 times table (5, 10, 15 and so on), and 12 isn’t in it. So nothing except 1 goes into both.
steps.wrong: Not quite. If nothing goes into both numbers, the fraction is already simple, so type 5/12 again.
steps.why: 5 and 12 have nothing in common except 1, so 5/12 can’t be simplified. That means 1/4 + 1/6 = 5/12.

parts.title: On your own
parts.intro: This time I’ll stay out of the way. Add 3/10 + 1/6 with the four moves. Tap Hint if you get stuck.
parts.finish: You did it on your own: 3/10 + 1/6 = 7/15. Common denominator, convert, add the tops, simplify. The same four moves work for any two fractions.

steps.multipleNote: {n} works too, but the smallest is 30, so we’ll use that.

mistakes.say: 16 is 10 + 6, but adding the bottoms doesn’t make a common denominator. You need a number that both 10 and 6 go into.
6 doesn’t go into 10 evenly. Try counting up in tens and test each number with 6.
10 doesn’t go into 6. You need a bigger number.

hints: Count up in tens: 10, 20, 30. Which one does 6 go into?
steps.wrong: Not quite. The number has to be in both the 10 times table and the 6 times table.
steps.why: 30 is in the 10 times table (10 × 3) and in the 6 times table (6 × 5).

steps.say: Move 2: rewrite 3/10 with the common denominator.
steps.ifEquivalent: That’s the same amount, but we need 30 on the bottom so the fractions can be added.

mistakes.say: You changed the bottom to 30 but left the top as 3. Whatever you multiply the bottom by, multiply the top by as well.

hints: What do you multiply 10 by to get 30?
steps.wrong: Not quite. Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number to get 30 on the bottom.
steps.why: 10 × 3 = 30, so the top is 3 × 3 = 9. That makes 3/10 = 9/30.

steps.ifEquivalent: That’s the same amount, but we need 30 on the bottom so the fractions can be added.

mistakes.say: You changed the bottom to 30 but left the top as 1. Whatever you multiply the bottom by, multiply the top by as well.

hints: What do you multiply 6 by to get 30?
steps.wrong: Not quite. Multiply the top and the bottom by the same number to get 30 on the bottom.
steps.why: 6 × 5 = 30, so the top is 1 × 5 = 5. That makes 1/6 = 5/30.

steps.ifEquivalent: That’s the same amount, but this line is the plain sum before simplifying. Keep 30 on the bottom.

mistakes.say: Careful: when the pieces are the same size, the bottom stays the same. Only the tops are added.

hints: Add the tops: 9 + 5. The bottom stays as it is.
steps.wrong: Not quite. Add the tops and keep the bottom the same.
steps.why: 9 + 5 = 14, and the bottom stays 30, because we’re still counting thirtieths.

steps.ifEquivalent: That’s the same amount, but it can be simpler. Look for a number that goes into both the top and the bottom.
hints: Both 14 and 30 are even. What can you divide both by?
Divide the top and the bottom by 2: 14 ÷ 2 and 30 ÷ 2.
7 and 15 have nothing in common except 1, so you stop there.
steps.wrong: Not quite. Divide the top and the bottom by the same number.
steps.why: Both numbers divide by 2: 14 ÷ 2 = 7 and 30 ÷ 2 = 15. Nothing else goes into both 7 and 15, so 7/15 is as simple as it gets.
